A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NashPG research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C are readable and support comparison. Revised evaluation settings limit direct performance comparisons but do not prevent assessing the revision.

before.justification: V1 reports original exploitability and Elo experiments across seven games, regularization experiments, and runtime and memory measurements.

after.justification: V2 reports original exploitability and head-to-head results, expanded regularization experiments, and a controlled comparison of R-NaD with its PPO variant.

M1.justification: The proposed objectives in Equations 11–12 and NashPG's sampled policy-gradient, KL-regularization, and reference-update procedure are retained. IMMD renames v1's MMD-based iterative M method. RNaD-PPO is introduced as an experimental comparator.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven game tasks: Kuhn Poker, Leduc Poker, Dark Hex, Phantom Tic-Tac-Toe, Liar's Dice, Battleship, and Heads-Up NLHE. V2's ADH3 and APTTT names identify the abrupt variants already specified in v1 Appendix B.3.

E2.justification: V2 adds R-NaD to the main comparisons alongside the retained NFSP, PSRO, and MMD baselines. Section 5.4 additionally evaluates RNaD-PPO, while the regularization comparison now includes MMD and R-NaD rather than only NashPG as in v1 Table 1.

E3.justification: Reported evaluation switches from PPO best-response approximations to exact exploitability for four smaller games; large-game exploiter training increases from 2,000 steps to 10,000 updates. Elo tournaments are replaced by 1,024-game final-policy comparisons. Training budgets become 250,000 updates outside Kuhn Poker, versus 50,000 or 100,000 previously. PPO settings and model configurations also change, including entropy coefficient 0.05 to 0.1 and NLHE hidden dimension 256 to 512.

E4.justification: V2 broadens the regularization study beyond v1's three NashPG coefficients, adds learning trajectories and the seven-game NeuRD-to-PPO ablation, and introduces game-complexity analysis. V1's runtime and memory analysis is removed. The annealing experiment in Appendix C.1 is retained, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report four independent runs or random seeds and means with standard deviations. V2 extends this existing practice to its new results without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests, or a different repeated-run count.

E6.justification: The main exploitability curves are replaced under revised settings, and new regularization, R-NaD, and optimizer-ablation results are reported. V2 Table 3 adds head-to-head payoffs, including NashPG versus R-NaD at +0.098 ± 0.072 in Heads-Up Poker. V1's Elo results and runtime/memory measurements are removed. These changes do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The main variational-inequality definitions, assumptions, convergence results, and Appendix A proofs retain their mathematical substance. V2 Appendix B.2 adds supplementary combinatorial derivations and information-state bounds for the larger games, absent from v1's complexity summaries.

C1.justification: The claimed research gap is substantially reframed: v1 emphasizes fixed-strength refinement as an alternative to decaying regularization, whereas v2 acknowledges existing multi-round methods and centers the policy-gradient optimization design. The headline large-game claim changes from higher Elo ratings to higher head-to-head payoffs. The underlying monotonic-convergence claim is retained.

C2.justification: V2 explains the regularization response through stability, bias, and refinement speed, and attributes much of R-NaD's performance gap to its inner optimizer. Section 4.3 explicitly identifies why practical NashPG lacks the theoretical guarantee. V2 also replaces v1's strong warning about unreliable large-game exploitability with an argument that agreement with head-to-head results makes approximate evaluation informative.

D1.justification: V2 documents exact-evaluation interfaces, information-state enumeration, R-NaD implementation, and PSRO distillation, and revises the configuration tables. V1's hardware disclosure is removed; the code-access link is unchanged. Reproducibility remains limited by conflicting v2 settings: MMD's coefficient is 0.2 in Section 5.2 but 0.05 in Appendix B.3, and Liar's Dice history length is 32 in Table 5 but 16 in Appendix B.1.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a dedicated multi-round regularization category and a substantive comparison with APMD, DRDA, and R-NaD. New APMD, DRDA, and NeuRD references support this positioning. Perolat's 2021 work and Rudolph's policy-gradient reevaluation, already cited in v1, become central antecedents and motivation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experiments, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around four questions, Appendix B is reordered and expanded, and IMMD terminology clarifies the theoretical/practical distinction. The title, author block, and algorithm numbering also change.

P2.justification: V2 introduces method-comparison, complexity, and head-to-head tables, new sensitivity plots, and an optimizer-ablation figure. Benchmark plots are redrawn with revised axes and legends. The Elo and resource figures disappear, while the retained annealing plot moves from Figure 4 to Figure 6. Appendix table structures and placement also change.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidentiary gaps by evaluating the closely related R-NaD baseline, testing its inner optimizer through a controlled ablation, and reporting exact exploitability for the smaller games. Its clearer separation of IMMD's guarantee from practical NashPG also improves claim precision. These substantial gains outweigh the loss of resource analysis, although conflicting MMD and Liar's Dice settings still limit reproducibility.
